why_how.text: Backing and opening a door each come with a specific look before you move.
Where you park, how you set your wheels on a hill and where parking is banned are all spelled out.

scenario.text: Pia parks facing downhill on a street with a curb.

reasoning.text: Where a curb exists on a hill, aim the front wheels right when parked facing downhill.

result.text: Pia turns her front wheels right, toward the curb.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the wheels always point the same way on any hill.

correction.text: Hills with a curb split wheel direction by grade, left up and right down, while hills without a curb always point wheels right.

memory_support.text: Curb uphill left, downhill right; no curb, always right.

prompt.text: Pia parks facing downhill next to a curb. Which way should her front wheels point?

rationale.text: With a curb, wheels aim left facing uphill and right facing downhill; without a curb, they always point right.

lines.text: How to back up.
Before you open a door.
Where and how to park.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on backing, exiting and parking. We start with backing up, where the manual names the most common mistake drivers make, and then the scan you make before swinging a car door open. Then we cover where to park on the road, how to set your front wheels when parking on a hill with a curb and without one, and the long list of places and distances where parking is banned. The hill parking rules and the distance bans are the parts most packed with details, so we will take them slowly and set them side by side. By the end of the lesson you should be able to park correctly on any street the manual describes.

lines.text: Most common mistake: not looking both ways behind.
Twist body and head right; look through the rear window.
Scan for cars, bikes and walkers before opening a door.

narration.text: Drivers backing up most often fail to look both ways behind them. Mirrors leave gaps, so twist your body and head to the right to look through the rear window, reverse slowly, and glance to each side for walkers and traffic. Before swinging a door open, scan for cars, bicyclists and pedestrians around the parked vehicle. Put as a contrast: backing needs a body twist to the rear window with slow reversing, while exiting only needs a scan for cars, bikes and walkers before the door swings. Both moves start with a look, but backing asks for more, because mirrors leave gaps.

lines.text: As far from traffic as the road allows.
Within one foot of a curb.
Two-way: right side. One-way: either side.

narration.text: Park as far from traffic as the road allows. Pull deep onto shoulders, and park tight to curbs, within one foot. On two-way streets, park on the right. On one-way roads, you may park on either side. Put as a contrast: two-way streets park right only, while one-way roads park either side. The one-foot rule is the number to remember for curb parking on a flat street. On a hill, you still park close to the curb, but you also set your front wheels in a particular direction, which is the subject of the next slide. Curb parking hugs within one foot on the flat, while hill parking with a curb angles the wheels.

lines.text: Set wheels to block a streetward roll.
Facing uphill: wheels left.
Facing downhill: wheels right.

narration.text: Where a curb exists on a hill, set the front wheels so that the car cannot roll into the street. Aim them left when you are parked facing uphill, and right when you are parked facing downhill. So with a curb, the wheel direction depends on the grade: left facing uphill, right facing downhill. Curb parking hugs within one foot on the flat, while hill parking with a curb angles the wheels left uphill and right downhill. The purpose stated in the manual is to block a roll toward the street. Learn the two cases as a pair, because the exam can ask about either one, and the other case, a hill without a curb, comes next.

lines.text: No curb on a hill: wheels right.
Uphill or downhill, the same.
Any roll sends the rear away from traffic.

narration.text: Here is the trap. It is easy to learn the uphill and downhill rule for curbs and then apply it to every hill. Without a curb, the rule is different. Point the front wheels right, so any roll sends the rear of the car away from traffic, whether you are facing uphill or downhill. Hills with a curb split wheel direction by grade, left up and right down, while hills without a curb always point the wheels right. So the first question to ask on a hill is whether there is a curb. If there is, check whether you face uphill or downhill. If there is not, the answer is always right, and the grade does not change it.

lines.text: Beside a parked vehicle; crosswalks; sidewalks.
Ahead of driveways; yellow curbs; No Parking signs.
Disabled spaces and aisles; bike lanes; blocking a lane.

narration.text: Parking is banned in many places. You may not park beside another parked vehicle, on crosswalks or sidewalks, ahead of driveways, at yellow curbs or No Parking signs, in disabled spaces or their striped aisles, on the hard road surface where no curb runs, in bike lanes, or anywhere the car blocks or endangers a traffic lane. Then there are distance bans. Keep clear within fifteen feet of hydrants, within twenty feet of intersections, within fifteen feet of fire, ambulance or rescue station entrances, within five hundred feet of fire equipment working an alarm, and within fifty feet of railroad crossings.

lines.text: Facing downhill.
Curb present.
Which way do the wheels point?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Pia parks facing downhill on a street with a curb. Which way should her front wheels point? Work it out before reading on. The answer is right. Where a curb exists on a hill, the front wheels aim left when parked facing uphill and right when parked facing downhill. If Pia were on a hill with no curb, the answer would also be right, because without a curb the wheels always point right. The case where the answer is left is the uphill case with a curb. Ask first whether there is a curb, then which way the car faces. Curb uphill left, downhill right; no curb, always right.

lines.text: Back with a body twist; scan before doors.
One foot from the curb; right on two-way streets.
Know the place and distance bans.

narration.text: To close the lesson: back up by twisting your body and head to the right, looking through the rear window, reversing slowly, and glancing to each side. Scan for cars, bicyclists and pedestrians before opening a door. Park as far from traffic as the road allows, within one foot of a curb, on the right of two-way streets and on either side of one-way roads. On a hill with a curb, aim the wheels left uphill and right downhill; without a curb, always right. Some parking bans name places like crosswalks and driveways, while others name distances like fifteen feet from hydrants and twenty feet from intersections.

why_how.text: Most crashes trace to missed risks, so you scan around you and use headlights when sight is poor.
Low-beams, high-beams, glare and fog each have their own rule.

scenario.text: Hal drives on a dark highway and comes up behind another car.

reasoning.text: Take low-beams within two hundred feet behind another vehicle.

result.text: Hal switches to low-beams before he is within two hundred feet of the car ahead.

claim.text: Common mistake: using high-beams in fog to see farther.

correction.text: Fog throws your own beams back at you, so drop to low-beams in thick fog, steer by edge markings and slow down.

memory_support.text: Low close, high only on open road.

prompt.text: Hal is following a car on a dark highway. When must he switch to low-beams?

answer.text: Within two hundred feet behind the other vehicle.

rationale.text: Low-beams serve towns, oncoming meetings and close following inside two hundred feet.

lines.text: Scan for risks.
Headlights by law.
Beams, glare and fog.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on seeing and being seen. Crashes trace most to missed risks, so the manual asks you to keep track of the vehicles around you, scan ahead, to the sides and behind, and stay ready for walkers and cyclists. It also sets clear rules for headlights: when state law requires them, when to use low-beams and when high-beams are allowed, what to do about an oncoming driver who keeps high-beams on, and how to drive in fog. Several of these rules come with distances, five hundred feet and two hundred feet, so listen for which distance belongs to which rule.

lines.text: Track vehicles; scan ahead, sides and behind.
Headlights at night and in poor sight.
Required when sight drops to five hundred feet or wipers run.

narration.text: Crashes trace most to missed risks. Keep track of the vehicles around you, scan ahead, to the sides and behind, stay ready for walkers and cyclists, and switch headlights on at night and in poor sight. State law demands headlights in rain, fog, snow or sleet once sight drops to five hundred feet, and whenever your wipers run for bad weather. Burning headlights even by day makes you easier for others to see. Put as a contrast: scanning covers ahead, sides and behind for missed risks, while headlights cover night and poor sight, including wipers-on weather. The simplest test to remember is: wipers on for weather, headlights on.

lines.text: Headlights from sunset to sunrise.
Low-beams: lit towns, oncoming traffic, within two hundred feet behind.
High-beams: highways clear of oncoming within five hundred feet.

narration.text: Burn headlights from sunset to sunrise, and from the first fading light. Use low-beams in lit towns, against oncoming traffic, and within two hundred feet behind another vehicle. Save high-beams for highways with no approaching vehicles within five hundred feet. Put as a contrast: low-beams serve towns, oncoming meetings and close following inside two hundred feet, while high-beams serve open highway free of oncoming vehicles inside five hundred feet. So two hundred feet is the following distance for switching to low-beams, and five hundred feet is the oncoming distance that rules out high-beams. Keep the two numbers attached to their situations.

lines.text: Oncoming high-beams: look to the road edge.
Never flash your high-beams back.
Fog: low-beams, edge markings, slower speed.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two situations tempt drivers to use high-beams, and the manual says no to both. When an oncoming driver keeps high-beams on, avert your stare toward the road edge, glance ahead to fix the other car's place, and repeat until you are past it. Never fire your own high-beams back. In fog, your own beams are thrown back at you, so drop to low-beams in thick fog, steer by the edge markings, and slow down, since even thin fog warps distance judgment. So oncoming glare calls for edge glances without high-beam revenge, while fog calls for low-beams with edge-marking steering and slower speed.

lines.text: Five hundred feet: headlights required in bad weather.
Five hundred feet: no high-beams with oncoming vehicles.
Two hundred feet: low-beams when following.

narration.text: Here are the distances from this lesson together. State law demands headlights in rain, fog, snow or sleet once sight drops to five hundred feet. High-beams are reserved for highways with no approaching vehicles within five hundred feet. And low-beams are required within two hundred feet behind another vehicle. So five hundred feet appears twice, once for when bad weather makes headlights required, and once for oncoming vehicles and high-beams, while two hundred feet belongs to following another car. Add the time rule as well: headlights from sunset to sunrise and from the first fading light, and whenever your wipers run for bad weather.

lines.text: Dark highway.
Following another car.
When do you switch to low-beams?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Hal is driving on a dark highway with high-beams on, and he comes up behind another car. When must he switch to low-beams? Work it out before reading on. The answer is within two hundred feet behind the other vehicle. Low-beams serve lit towns, oncoming meetings, and close following inside two hundred feet, while high-beams serve open highway with no approaching vehicles within five hundred feet. If a car were approaching from the other direction, the distance to remember would be five hundred feet. And if fog rolled in, Hal would drop to low-beams, steer by the edge markings and slow down. Low close, high only on open road.

lines.text: Scan ahead, sides, behind.
Headlights in poor sight and with wipers.
Low-beams close; never flash back; low in fog.

narration.text: To close the lesson: crashes trace most to missed risks, so track the vehicles around you and scan ahead, to the sides and behind. State law requires headlights in rain, fog, snow or sleet once sight drops to five hundred feet, and whenever wipers run for bad weather. Burn headlights from sunset to sunrise. Use low-beams in lit towns, against oncoming traffic and within two hundred feet behind another vehicle, and save high-beams for highways with no approaching vehicles within five hundred feet. Against stubborn high-beams, look toward the road edge and never flash back. In thick fog, use low-beams, steer by the edge markings and slow down.

why_how.text: Fading sight and slick pavement call for slowing first, doubling the gap and lighting the headlamps.
Rain, snow and ice each bring specific rules about traction, clearing the car and braking.

scenario.text: Rain begins to fall after a long dry spell, and Eva is driving to work.

reasoning.text: Treat the first half-hour as slickest, because oil mixes with water, and shun ponded water where the car can hydroplane.

result.text: Eva slows down, runs her low-beams and avoids standing water.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking hard to stop on a sheet of ice.

correction.text: To halt on slick sheets, ease off the gas with gentle braking, since rolling front tires grip best and steady slowness beats hard braking.

memory_support.text: Slow, double the gap, lights on.

prompt.text: Rain has just started. When is the road slickest?

answer.text: In the first half-hour, as oil mixes with water.

rationale.text: Rain strikes slickest in the first half-hour of oil mixing, while snow demands full clearing before rolling.

lines.text: Poor sight and slick pavement.
Rain and hydroplaning.
Snow, ice and braking.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on rain, snow and ice. The manual's general rule for fading sight and slick pavement is to slow first, double the normal gap ahead, and turn on your headlights. Then it gives specific rules for rain, including when the road is slickest and the danger of ponded water, for snow and ice, including clearing the whole car before you drive, and for braking and stopping on packed snow and ice. Each of these rules is short, and several of them include a time or a doubling that is easy to remember once you have it. We will finish with the braking rule for ice.

lines.text: Slow down first.
Double the normal gap ahead.
Turn on the headlamps.

narration.text: When sight fades or the pavement turns slick, the manual's response is the same three steps. Slow down first. Double the normal gap ahead. And light the headlamps. The order matters: slowing comes first, then the bigger gap, then the lights. This rule applies to every hazardous condition in this lesson, rain, snow and ice, and it connects to the braking rule at the end. Slick sheets call for gentle braking with rolling front tires, matching the hazard rule that doubles the normal gap. So whenever the weather makes the road slick or hard to see, think of these three steps together: slow, double the gap, lights on.

lines.text: Low-beams; wipers with fluid ready.
First half-hour is slickest: oil mixes with water.
Avoid ponded water: hydroplaning.

narration.text: In rain, run your low-beams. Wipe light rain and drizzle with washer fluid ready, since dry sprinkles smear the glass. Treat the first half-hour as the slickest, because oil on the road mixes with the water. And avoid ponded water, where the car can hydroplane and lose control. So rain strikes slickest in the first half-hour of oil mixing, while snow demands full clearing before rolling and chains or snow tires for grip. Standing water is the other rain hazard the manual names, because the car can hydroplane and lose control in it.

lines.text: Clear every trace of snow and ice first.
Roof, hood, tail, glass, mirrors, all lamps.
Snow tires or chains for grip.

narration.text: Before you drive in snow or ice, strip every trace of snow and ice from the car: the roof, hood and tail, the glass, the mirrors and all the lamps. Shed slabs of snow and ice menace other drivers. Fit snow tires or chains to grip the road and shorten stops. Treat packed snow like ice. Brake softly, and shed speed before stops and turns. Expect bridges and shaded areas to ice first. So you clear the car because shed slabs menace others, and snow tires or chains help you grip and stop. The next slide covers the hardest part of winter driving, which is stopping on a slick sheet of ice.

lines.text: Ease off the gas; brake gently.
Rolling front tires grip best.
Steady slowness beats hard braking.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Hard braking on ice is the mistake the manual warns against. To halt on slick sheets, ease off the gas with gentle braking, since rolling front tires grip best, and steady slowness beats hard braking. Treat packed snow like ice, brake softly, and shed speed before stops and turns. Expect bridges and shade to ice first. Slick sheets want gentle braking with rolling front tires, matching the hazard rule that doubles the normal gap. So the plan on ice is to arrive slowly, with plenty of room, and to stop gently, rather than to rely on hard braking at the last moment.

lines.text: Rain has just started.
When is the road slickest?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: rain has just started after a dry spell. When is the road slickest? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the first half-hour, as oil on the road mixes with the water. In rain, run low-beams, keep washer fluid ready, and shun ponded water where the car can hydroplane and lose control. Remember the general rule for any slick condition as well: slow first, double the normal gap, and turn on your headlights. And if the rain turns to ice, ease off the gas and brake gently, because rolling front tires grip best. Slow, double the gap, lights on.

lines.text: Slow, double the gap, lights on.
Rain: first half-hour slickest; avoid ponds.
Snow: clear it all; ice: brake gently.

narration.text: To close the lesson: in fading sight or on slick pavement, slow first, double the normal gap ahead and turn on the headlamps. In rain, run low-beams, keep washer fluid ready, treat the first half-hour as slickest, and avoid ponded water where the car can hydroplane. Before driving in snow, clear every trace of snow and ice from the roof, hood, tail, glass, mirrors and lamps, and fit snow tires or chains. Treat packed snow like ice, brake softly, and expect bridges and shade to ice first. To stop on ice, ease off the gas with gentle braking, since rolling front tires grip best. Slow, double the gap, lights on.

why_how.text: Virginia law defines aggressive driving by intent plus a traffic violation.
The manual lists aggressive behaviors, how to respond to them and the license penalty for a conviction.

scenario.text: A driver tailgates Ben, flashes lights and honks to push him out of the lane.

reasoning.text: Counter aggressors by yielding space, refusing races and stares, and ignoring the noise.

result.text: Ben moves over when it is safe, does not look at the driver, and lets them go.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any fast driving counts as aggressive driving under the law.

correction.text: The law defines aggression by harassing intent plus an offense, while the behavior list names the offenses from sign-running to shoulder passing.

prompt.text: Theo is convicted of aggressive driving. What range of license suspension does he face?

answer.text: From ten days up to six months.

rationale.text: Courts answer aggressive-driving convictions with ten days to six months of suspension.

lines.text: What the law says.
What aggressors do.
How to respond.

narration.text: Welcome to the last lesson of this section, on aggressive driving. Virginia law defines aggressive driving, and the manual lists the behaviors that aggressive drivers show. It also tells you how to respond when you meet one: give them space, refuse to race or stare back, and ignore the noise. And it gives the penalty for a conviction, which can include a license suspension. In this lesson we cover the legal definition, the behavior list, the right response, and the length of the suspension. The definition has two parts that must both be present.

lines.text: Aiming to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct.
While breaking traffic rules.
Skipping stops, yields, controls or room for overtakers.

narration.text: Virginia law brands aggressive driving as aiming to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct someone while breaking traffic rules. The examples of rules include skipping stops, skipping yields, ignoring traffic control devices, or not giving room to drivers who are overtaking. So the definition has two parts: an intent, which is to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct, and an offense, which is breaking a traffic rule. Put as a contrast: the law defines aggression by harassing intent plus an offense, while the behavior list names the offenses, from sign-running to shoulder passing. Both parts of the definition must be present for the legal meaning to apply.

lines.text: Run signs and signals; speed; tailgate; weave.
Pass on the right, even on shoulders and unpaved edges.
Change lanes wildly; gesture, scream, honk, flash.

narration.text: Aggressive drivers run signs and signals, speed, tailgate and weave. They pass on the right, even on shoulders and unpaved edges, change lanes wildly, and gesture, scream, honk and flash their lights. That is the behavior list. Counter it by yielding space, refusing races and stares, and ignoring the noise. So the manual's response is to step out of the contest: let the aggressive driver go, do not race, do not lock eyes, and do not react to the honking or gestures. Drivers answer aggressors with space and ignored noise. The courts have their own answer for a conviction, which is the subject of the next slide.

lines.text: Conviction can suspend a license.
From ten days.
Up to six months.

narration.text: Here is the trap: the suspension range has two numbers, and they are easy to misremember. An aggressive-driving conviction can suspend a license for ten days, or for as long as six months. So the shortest suspension is ten days and the longest is six months. Put as a contrast: drivers answer aggressors with space and ignored noise, while courts answer convictions with ten days to six months of suspension. If an exam question offers a range, look for ten days at the low end and six months at the high end. Any answer with years, or with no suspension at all, does not match the rule in the manual.

lines.text: Aggressive-driving conviction.
How long a suspension?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver is convicted of aggressive driving. How long can the license be suspended? Work it out before reading on. The answer is from ten days up to six months. An aggressive-driving conviction can suspend a license for ten days or as long as six months. Remember also what makes driving aggressive under Virginia law: aiming to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct someone while breaking traffic rules. And remember how to respond when you meet an aggressive driver: yield space, refuse races and stares, and ignore the noise. Give space, skip the stare, and let the courts handle the conviction.

lines.text: Intent plus a traffic violation.
Yield space; refuse races and stares.
Ten days to six months.

narration.text: To close the section: Virginia law defines aggressive driving as aiming to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct someone while breaking traffic rules, such as skipping stops, yields or control devices, or not leaving room for overtakers. Aggressive drivers run signs and signals, speed, tailgate, weave, pass on the right even on shoulders, change lanes wildly, and gesture, scream, honk and flash. Counter them by yielding space, refusing races and stares, and ignoring the noise. An aggressive-driving conviction can suspend a license for ten days or as long as six months. The memory line for meeting an aggressor is: give space, skip the stare.
